summary: Djibouti requires nearly every foreign visitor to obtain an eVisa through the official government portal before travel — short-stay eVisas cover up to 14 days and standard ones up to 90 — as visas on arrival are no longer routinely issued.

passportValidity.text: Your passport should be valid for at least 6 months on arrival in Djibouti.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.certificate: International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis (yellow card)
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever certificate is required from travelers arriving from countries with a risk of yellow fever transmission — relevant if you arrive overland or via much of sub-Saharan Africa.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Djibouti entry requirements

travelInsurance.text: No official source we could find states whether travel insurance is required to enter Djibouti. Medical facilities are limited and evacuation is expensive, so cover with medical evacuation is worth having.

onwardTicket.text: The eVisa application asks for a flight reservation (or other means of transport), an accommodation address (hotel or host) and an invitation letter.

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published. The e-Visa application asks for a flight reservation, an accommodation address (hotel or host) and an invitation letter, but no official source states a funds requirement.

notes: The UK Foreign Office says photographing infrastructure such as ports, public buildings, airports, military facilities and bridges is prohibited; your equipment could be confiscated and you could be arrested.

payments.text: The UK Foreign Office says credit and debit cards are not widely accepted, and where they are you often need a Visa card. ATMs are normally available in Djibouti City but may not accept Mastercard, so carry enough cash.

safety.text: The UK advises against all travel to the Djibouti–Eritrea border. Elsewhere the main risk is petty crime, so keep valuables, particularly cameras and passports, out of sight, and avoid travelling outside city centres after dark.

tips.text: Arrive with your eVisa approval already printed or saved. Visas on arrival have been largely phased out and airlines check for the eVisa at check-in.
The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to the Djibouti–Eritrea border, and Canada advises against non-essential travel within 10 km of it. There are unmarked landmines near the border.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Djibouti?
faq.answer: Almost certainly yes — Djibouti requires nearly every foreign nationality to obtain an eVisa before travel through the official portal evisa.gouv.dj. A short-stay eVisa covers up to 14 days and a standard one up to 90 days.

faq.question: Can I get a visa on arrival in Djibouti?
faq.answer: Do not plan on it. Djibouti has shifted visa issuance to the online eVisa system, and airlines generally require the approval before boarding. Apply on evisa.gouv.dj a few days before departure.

faq.question: How much does the Djibouti eVisa cost?
faq.answer: The official eVisa portal lists USD 12 for a visa of up to 14 days and USD 23 for a stay of 15 to 90 days, plus 10% VAT added at payment.
